name: Artemas
title: Paul's coworker
summary: Artemas is a Christian coworker mentioned in Paul's letter to Titus. In Tit 3:12 it appears that Paul considered sending either Artemas or Tychicus to Crete to take over Titus' responsibility there, so that Titus could join Paul in Nicopolis. Although Artemas is only mentioned in this one place in the New Testament, the context testifies that he was a trusted and competent leader whom Paul regarded as fit to carry out church work. His name suggests Greek origin, and he was part of a broader network of traveling coworkers who were crucial for the spread of the Christian faith throughout the Mediterranean region.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned as a possible envoy to Crete
keyEvents.description: Paul writes to Titus that he plans to send either Artemas or Tychicus to Crete to relieve him. The purpose was for Titus to be able to travel on to Nicopolis in Epirus, where Paul planned to spend the winter.

keyEvents.title: Part of Paul's network of coworkers
keyEvents.description: In the closing of the letter to Titus, Artemas is mentioned alongside other trusted coworkers such as Tychicus, Zenas, and Apollos. The context paints a picture of an active network of servants who worked together to establish and strengthen churches around the Mediterranean.

versions.summary: Artemas was one of the apostle Paul's trusted coworkers in the early church. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Paul's letter to Titus, where Paul plans to send either Artemas or Tychicus to Crete to relieve Titus. Although little is known about him, the mention shows that he was a reliable and trusted person in Paul's missionary service.
versions.title: Paul's coworker
versions.reason: [minor] The role 'disciple' is acceptable, but 'leader' is somewhat speculative. The Bible does not explicitly state that Artemas was a leader – only that Paul planned to send him to Crete. The roles 'co-worker' or 'messenger' would have been more precise. 'Leader' can be retained as implicit (he was to replace Titus), but 'co-worker' should be added.; [minor] The four events overlap significantly – all refer to Titus 3:12-14. The last two events ('Connection to Paul's network of co-workers' and 'Service in the early church') are more interpretations and summaries than distinct events. It would have been more precise to combine them or reduce them to fewer, more distinct events.; [minor] The description refers to Artemas as one of 'the many unnamed believers', but Artemas is actually named in the Bible, so the wording is somewhat misleading.; [major] Footnotes are missing. For a profile like Artemas, information about the etymology of the name (Greek origin, possible connection to the goddess Artemis) should be included, as well as early church traditions about him.

Since there is an earlier version, the text should be rephrased to avoid repetition and provide a fresher presentation.; [minor] The second key event ('Part of Paul's network of coworkers') is more of a contextual observation than a specific event. footnotes.text: The name Artemas (Greek: Ἀρτεμᾶς) is likely a short form of Artemidoros, meaning 'gift from Artemis'. This was a common Greek name in antiquity, suggesting that Artemas had a Greco-pagan background before becoming a Christian believer.

According to some early church traditions, including the so-called 'list of the seventy disciples' (attributed to Pseudo-Dorotheus from the 5th century), Artemas is said to have become bishop in Lystra. This tradition is late and cannot be verified historically, but it shows that later Christians wished to honor his memory.

Nicopolis, where Paul planned to spend the winter (Tit 3:12), was a city founded by Emperor Augustus in Epirus (northwestern Greece) to commemorate the victory at Actium in 31 BC. The city was an important cultural and strategic hub, and Paul's desire to winter there may indicate that he planned further missionary work in the region.

The fact that Paul could choose between Artemas and Tychicus as Titus' replacement on Crete shows a flexible organizational structure in the early Pauline mission. Workers were sent where the need was greatest, and this pattern has similarities with the traveling apostolic ministry described in the Didache, an early Christian document from the end of the first century.
